articles.title: Watch: SpaceX launches crew to International Space Station
articles.summary: The Falcon 9 rocket blasted off from Cape Canaveral with two Americans, a Russian and a Canadian who will spend up to six months aboard the International Space Station.
articles.body:
The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launched from Cap Canaveral, Florida to the International Space Station carrying Crew-13. The team is comprised of two Nasa astronauts, a Russian cosmonaut and a Canadian astronaut whose wife is expecting their third child two months into the mission. They'll become the fourth couple in the history of space travel to have a child born while one parent was off the planet, according to CBSNews.

The launch was originally planned for mid-September, but was delayed to replace a valve in the Crew Dragon's propulsion system. It will take 7 hours and 50 minutes for the crew to reach the ISS where they will be conducting experiments and research toward future missions to the Moon and Mars, according to Nasa.

articles.title: Google has a ‘moonshot’ plan for AI data centers in space
articles.summary: Google’s AI datacenter “moonshot” plan would build up its infrastructure of TPU chips in space where they could draw power from the sun nearly 24/7.
articles.body: Google has dreamed up a potential new way to get around resource constraints for energy-hungry AI data centers on Earth — launching its AI chips into space on solar-powered satellites. It’s a ‘moonshot’ research project Google announced today called Project Suncatcher. If it can ever get off the ground, the project would essentially create space-based data centers. Google hopes that by doing so, it can harness solar power around-the-clock. The dream is harnessing a near-unlimited source of clean energy that might allow the company to chase its AI ambitions without the concerns its data centers on Earth have raised when it comes to driving up power plant emissions and utility bills through soaring electricity demand. “In the future, space may be the best place to scale AI compute,” Travis Beals, a Google senior director for Paradigms of Intelligence, writes in a blog post today. The company also published a preprint paper, which has not undergone academic peer review, detailing its progress so far on this endeavor. There are major hurdles Google would need to overcome to turn this plan into reality, which it explains in the blog and paper. Google envisions its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) orbiting Earth on satellites outfitted with solar panels that could generate electricity almost continuously, making them eight times more productive than similar panels on Earth, according to Google. A major challenge will be to ensure that the satellites can communicate well with each other. Competing with data centers on land “requires links between satellites that support tens of terabits per second,” Google writes. Maneuvering constellations of satellites into tight formations can help them achieve that, perhaps flying satellites within “kilometers or less” of each other. That’s much closer than satellites operate today, and already space junk from collisions is a growing risk. On top of that, Google has to ensure that its TPUs can withstand higher levels of radiation in space. It has tested its Trillium TPUs for radiation tolerance and says they “survive a total ionizing dose equivalent to a 5 year mission life without permanent failures.” It would be pretty pricey to send those TPUs into space at the moment. But a cost analysis the company performed suggests that launching and running a data center in space could become “roughly comparable” to the energy costs of an equivalent data center on Earth on a per-kilowatt/year basis by the mid-2030s. Google says it’s planning a joint mission with the company Planet to launch a couple prototype satellites by 2027 in order to test its hardware in orbit.

articles.title: DoorDash is going airborne with new drone delivery division
articles.summary: DoorDash announced DoorDash Air, its new drone delivery division. The company received approval from the FAA to launch its own commercial service.
articles.body: DoorDash is launching a new drone delivery program called DoorDash Air. The largest food delivery app in the US said that it has approval from the Federal Aviation Administration that clears the way for drone delivery in the near future. DoorDash said it has received a Part 135 air carrier certification from the FAA that enable it to delivery small packages via drone. Other companies to receive this designation include Alphabet’s Wing, Zipline, and Amazon. Previously, DoorDash worked with Alphabet’s drone delivery division Wing on a number of pilots in places like Dallas-Fort Worth, Virginia, and Australia. Now the company says it will deploy its own drones, designed specifically for food delivery. The drones will be designed and assembled within the company’s DoorDash Labs division, which houses its robotics and AI teams responsible for building its Dot sidewalk delivery robots. “We’re designing an aircraft purpose-built for the gaps we see in local commerce, and it complements the short- and long-range designs our partners are scaling,” the company said in a press release. “Our drone is also proudly American-designed and built, with the majority of components made right here in the U.S.” (To be sure, the vast majority of drones are manufactured in China.) In addition, DoorDash says it will also build all the necessary ground-level infrastructure to enable restaurants to hand off their deliveries to drones. As seen with other drone delivery pilots, there is a complex system of structures and additional equipment that needs to be built on the ground to enable drones to pickup their payloads before embarking on their deliveries. And there are flight plans, airspace management, and drop-off logistics that needs to be established to track the drones in flight. DoorDash says its committed to building all that infrastructure itself. “The aircraft is what everyone sees,” the company says. “The harder problem is the infrastructure and integration on the ground, and that’s our advantage. Solving hard physical-world problems for local businesses is our focus, from real-time inventory reconciliation to universal handoff systems for drive-throughs, rooftops, or merchant back doors. We are building that complete end-to-end system.” DoorDash says drone delivery could solve the problem of midrange deliveries that still end up taking longer because couriers are hard to find. The company says more than 20 percent of its orders involve distances of three to five miles, but that those orders can take on average nearly 25 percent longer than shorter deliveries, largely because finding a courier takes longer for these mid-range trips. “Routing mid-range deliveries to drones lets Dashers focus on the orders they often favor: shorter deliveries that can be done quickly, staying near a high concentration of merchants for optimal routing, and maximizing their earning potential by getting them to their next order faster,” the company says. DoorDash didn’t reveal which markets it was targeting for its initial launch, noting that it would announce more details in the months to come.

articles.title: Sinal misterioso dá pistas sobre colisão de estrelas mortas | G1
articles.standfirst: Emissão permaneceu visível por quase 10 minutos e surpreendeu equipe que acompanhava o fenômeno. Um dos pesquisadores recebeu aviso em um trem sobre a explosão e começou, pelo computador, observações que ajudaram a esclarecer origem do sinal.
articles.summary: Emissão durou quase 10 minutos e surpreendeu pesquisadores. Um deles recebeu o aviso em um trem e iniciou pelo computador observações que ajudaram a explicar o fenômeno.
articles.body:
Representação artística mostra duas estrelas de nêutrons no momento da colisão, evento que pode produzir ondas gravitacionais e uma explosão de raios gama. — Foto: University of Warwick/Mark Garlick

Astrônomos encontraram fortes evidências de que um misterioso clarão de raios X , que durou quase dez minutos, foi produzido após a colisão de duas estrelas de nêutrons , restos extremamente densos de estrelas que chegaram ao fim de suas vidas.

O fenômeno, identificado como EP250704a/GRB 250704B , foi detectado em 4 de julho de 2025.

Primeiro, diferentes satélites registraram uma rápida explosão de raios gama, que durou menos de meio segundo. Logo depois, porém, o telescópio espacial Einstein Probe observou uma emissão de raios X que continuou por cerca de 560 segundos, pouco mais de nove minutos.

🛰️ ENTENDA : Raios gama são a forma mais energética de radiação eletromagnética e podem ser produzidos em eventos extremos do Universo, como essas colisões de estrelas de nêutrons. Quando aparecem em explosões muito rápidas, ajudam astrônomos a identificar fenômenos violentos e distantes.

Segundo os pesquisadores, essa foi a emissão imediata de raios X mais longa já observada em um evento desse tipo.

Os resultados foram publicados nesta quarta-feira (30) na revista científica "Science Bulletin".

Parte da investigação começou de forma pouco comum. Niccolò Passaleva, pesquisador da Universidade de Roma Tor Vergata e um dos autores do estudo, recebeu o aviso sobre a explosão quando voltava para casa.

“Eu estava voltando para casa de trem e, de repente, estava correndo contra o tempo para assumir um dos maiores telescópios do mundo pelo meu laptop”, relembrou Passaleva.

O equipamento era o Very Large Telescope (VLT), instalado no Chile. A rapidez era necessária porque o brilho deixado por fenômenos desse tipo diminui com o tempo e pode desaparecer antes que os astrônomos consigam reunir dados suficientes para descobrir sua origem.

Estrelas de nêutrons são restos deixados depois que estrelas muito massivas chegam ao fim de suas vidas.

Elas concentram uma enorme quantidade de matéria em uma região relativamente pequena e estão entre os objetos mais densos conhecidos no Universo.

Quando duas delas se aproximam e colidem, podem liberar grandes quantidades de energia e produzir ondas gravitacionais , deformações no espaço-tempo que viajam pelo Universo.

Até agora, uma das principais pistas usadas pelos astrônomos para identificar essas colisões eram os chamados surtos curtos de raios gama, explosões muito energéticas que normalmente duram menos de dois segundos.

Foi justamente um sinal desse tipo que apareceu no início do evento estudado. A explosão de raios gama durou cerca de 0,4 segundo.

Imagem do VLT mostra o brilho do evento EP250704a, ligado à colisão de estrelas de nêutrons. — Foto: Niccolò Passaleva, Eleonora Troja (ERC BHianca), ESO/VLT

O Einstein Probe detectou uma emissão de raios X que permaneceu ativa por quase dez minutos , muito além do clarão inicial.

A duração chamou atenção dos pesquisadores porque esse tipo de colisão costuma ser identificado por sinais muito mais rápidos.

Uma das hipóteses levantadas pela equipe é que o encontro tenha produzido um magnetar , um tipo de estrela de nêutrons que gira rapidamente e possui um campo magnético extremamente intenso .

Nesse caso, o objeto formado depois da colisão poderia continuar liberando energia e manter a emissão brilhante por mais tempo.

“Se o remanescente da colisão for um magnetar, ele pode continuar emitindo por mais tempo”, explicou Eleonora Troja, professora da Universidade de Roma Tor Vergata e uma das autoras do estudo.

Segundo ela, a energia associada ao campo magnético desse objeto pode ser transferida para o material ao redor e prolongar o brilho da explosão.

Para descobrir a origem do fenômeno, porém, os cientistas precisavam saber a que distância ele havia ocorrido.

Com as observações do VLT, a equipe conseguiu calcular a distância do evento: a luz da explosão viajou por mais de 6 bilhões de anos antes de chegar à Terra.

Os pesquisadores também procuraram sinais de uma supernova, outra possível explicação para esse tipo de emissão prolongada, mas não encontraram.

Desde o lançamento do Einstein Probe, em janeiro de 2024, astrônomos vêm detectando centenas de clarões rápidos de raios X em galáxias distantes.

Alguns já foram relacionados à morte de estrelas muito massivas, mas a origem de vários deles ainda não foi esclarecida.

O novo estudo sugere que parte desses sinais pode estar ligada a colisões de estrelas de nêutrons e que emissões prolongadas de raios X talvez sejam mais comuns nesses eventos do que se imaginava.

Os autores afirmam ainda que esse tipo de sinal pode ajudar na busca por fontes de ondas gravitacionais.

Se um clarão semelhante for identificado rapidamente, outros observatórios poderão procurar sinais vindos da mesma região do céu e tentar acompanhar o evento por diferentes caminhos.

“Encontrar mais desses clarões pode ajudar a revelar com que frequência fusões de estrelas de nêutrons produzem magnetares”, afirmou Passaleva.

Agora, o próximo passo da equipe é conseguir detectar, no mesmo evento, tanto uma emissão prolongada de raios X quanto as ondas gravitacionais produzidas pela colisão.

Isso permitiria aos cientistas acompanhar de forma mais direta o que acontece nos minutos seguintes ao encontro entre alguns dos objetos mais extremos do Universo.

Ilustração mostra satélite Einstein Probe observando emissão de raios X após colisão de estrelas de nêutrons. — Foto: Divulgação/Science Bulletin

articles.title: 2,100-year-old shipwreck filled with 122 varieties of ancient Roman tableware found by archaeologists in Turkey was mentioned in a letter by Roman statesman Cicero
articles.summary: Off the Turkish coast near Adrasan, marine archaeologists recently discovered the remains of an ancient cargo ship bound for Rome and loaded with
articles.body: Off the Turkish coast near Adrasan, marine archaeologists recently discovered the remains of an ancient cargo ship bound for Rome and loaded with thousands of pieces of tableware in 122 different varieties, most famous and in demand at the time. The vessel had been carrying ceramic plates, bowls and serving dishes when it sank some 2,100 years ago, as per a report by All Things Interesting.Researchers believe the cargo originated from the region around the ancient port city of Rhosus, in modern-day Arsuz, Turkey, which served as a hub for elite tableware production at the time. Rhosus tableware was so well known and in demand that the Roman statesman Marcus Tullius Cicero famously mentioned ordering it in a letter from 50 B.C.E.A shocking shipwreckAccording to an announcement about the discovery made by Turkey's Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, excavations on the shipwreck began in 2025. Since then, marine archaeologists have recovered thousands of ceramic pieces, which have been transferred either to the Antalya Museum or to conservation labs.The wreck, sitting at depths between 140 and 18 feet, revealed 122 distinct types of tableware of different forms and sizes. Due to the wreck's deep location, the team had to use underwater robotic systems to support the marine archaeologists' work on the ocean floor.The ship dates back 2,100 years and was transporting thousands of ceramics, packed together for shipment across the Mediterranean. The 122 distinct dish types also provide a detailed window into the variety of tableware available in the ancient world.Moreover, it reveals how ceramics were packed and distributed at the time. For instance, the ceramic pieces found in the shipwreck were packed with clay between them before being placed inside crates, in order to reduce the risk of them breaking while at sea.For the researchers, this packing method also aided in preserving the tableware for years after the ship sank, allowing modern experts to get insights from it that they might not otherwise be able to.Significance of Rhosus tablewareDuring the Late Hellenistic and Early Roman period, much of the Mediterranean's fine tableware was produced in the port of Rhosus in present-day Turkey. Historians are aware of this due to the various written records left behind by the Romans.Rhosus was mentioned, for instance, in a letter from the famous orator Cicero to his close friend Titus Pomponius Atticus, which he wrote while he was governor of Cilicia in about 50 B.C.E. In the note, Cicero wrote that he had ordered Rhosica vasa, which means vessels or dishes from Rhosus.In the centuries following the discovery of that short reference to these ceramics, archaeologists and scholars have debated the exact production site of Cicero’s tableware. Some scholars have suggested that Cicero’s ceramics may have been what’s known as Eastern Sigillata A, popular ancient clay tableware originating somewhere along the Gulf of İskenderun in southeastern Turkey, but the debate has continued.Although it remains unknown who ordered the newly found tableware shipment, the recent shipwreck discovery provides important physical evidence of the region's thriving maritime economy in ancient times. A similar shipwreck was also found filled with hundreds of well-preserved ceramics. Other marine archaeologists diving elsewhere in Turkey’s waters have also discovered a 1,500-year-old wreck carrying 10,000 ceramic plates, as well as a 1,100-year-old ship that sank with jugs of olive oil aboard.

articles.title: Scientists placed 23 3D-printed reefs up to 1,100 metres underwater to test whether damaged coral habitats can recover
articles.summary: Researchers are installing 3D-printed artificial reefs on the deep seabed to see whether damaged cold-water coral habitats can be restored.
articles.body: Researchers are installing 3D-printed artificial reefs on the deep seabed to see whether damaged cold-water coral habitats can be restored. Twenty-three of these structures have been placed off the south-west Porcupine Bank, off Ireland's west coast, and in the Bay of Biscay, France. The work forms part of the Horizon Europe project REDRESS, which stands for Restoration of deep-sea habitats to rebuild European Seas. According to the University of Galway, researchers are part of the international team behind the effort. The team wants to learn whether the structures can give corals a place to settle and grow in areas harmed by bottom trawling.How are scientists testing 3D-printed reefs underwaterThe twenty-three artificial reefs were installed as a contribution to REDRESS. The current campaign is part of a three-year mission known as REDECOR, short for REstauration DEs CORaux d'eau froide. It involves collaboration between researchers from the University of Galway, Ifremer and the Sorbonne University in France.The university states that the expedition took place on board L'Atalante, a vessel of the French Oceanographic Fleet, during August. Reefs were placed at depths between 900 and 1,100m off the Porcupine Bank and in the Guilvinec Canyon, Bay of Biscay, where other reefs installed during the 2025 expedition were also monitored. Monitoring of both Irish and French restoration sites is planned next year on board an Irish research vessel.Why are cold-water coral reefs important for deep-sea biodiversityCold-water coral reefs are regarded as less well known than their tropical cousins, but they provide important habitats for marine life and support biodiversity in the deep sea, including fish. The corals are quite fragile and easily damaged by deep-sea trawling. The university notes that recent fisheries and conservation regulations prohibit trawling in many areas where corals are found, and that the issue now is how to return damaged areas to full health.Dr Anthony Grehan, a deep-sea ecologist at University of Galway and co-leader of the mission to the Porcupine Bank, said: "These deep-sea coral reefs provide vital habitat for a diversity of marine life, but many have been damaged over many years. Because these corals grow by only a few millimetres each year, natural recovery of lost reefs can take decades to centuries."Marie-Claire Fabri, a research engineer in deep-sea benthic ecology at Ifremer and co-leader of the Bay of Biscay region expedition, said: "Preserving these areas alone is not enough; the active restoration of cold-water corals is urgently needed."How are the 3D-printed reefs designed to support coral growthThe artificial reefs are eco-designed cylinders made from low-carbon concrete incorporating volcanic material. Each 3D-printed structure is approximately 80cm high and 100cm in diameter, weighing around 600kg. They provide structurally complex physical microhabitats, including tunnels, ledges and overhangs, that offer shelter and provide surfaces for corals and other marine life to colonise. The reefs are placed individually on the seabed.The university explains that different approaches are being tested. Some reefs were equipped with oyster shells, ceramic plates and tiles to encourage coral larvae to settle naturally, while others were fitted with fragments, known as nubbins, of living coral. These fragments were collected from the ocean at depths of around 950 metres and kept in seawater tanks under conditions designed to replicate their natural environment. Small branches were then taken from the colonies and attached to oyster shells before being anchored on the artificial reefs. The team is focusing on the two principal reef-forming species of cold-water coral, Lophelia pertusa and Madrepora oculata.What marine species have colonised the artificial reefsResearchers found that the coral nubbins placed on the artificial reefs during the REDECOR 2025 mission are still alive. The reefs have also been colonised by a range of marine species, including sea urchins, fish, crabs and crinoids. Researchers will monitor the sites over the coming years through photography, video and 3D mapping, and will also monitor seawater conditions, sediment and chemical contaminants. The university says this will help improve understanding of the conditions needed for healthy coral growth and assess the potential impact of climate change and ocean acidification on restoration efforts.Dr Grehan said: "The early results are very encouraging, and if we can show that these approaches work, it could open up new possibilities to scale up the restoration of damaged coral reefs elsewhere in the Atlantic and beyond." According to the university, both restoration sites are now protected from bottom trawling. The SW Porcupine Bank site is protected under the European Common Fisheries Policy, where trawling is prohibited at depths greater than 800 metres, and the Guilvinec Canyon is a Natura 2000 site where trawling is also prohibited. REDRESS brings together 27 partners from 15 countries, and partners from the UK, Iceland and Italy have installed the same reef modules in their own restoration sites. The researchers expect the results to help inform implementation of the new European Nature Restoration Law.

articles.title: Scientists develop eDNA markers to detect Burmese pythons in southern Florida waters, but finding the snakes remains difficult
articles.summary: Scientists have developed and optimised python-specific environmental DNA (eDNA) markers to detect Burmese pythons through water samples collected in
articles.body: Scientists have developed and optimised python-specific environmental DNA (eDNA) markers to detect Burmese pythons through water samples collected in southern Florida. The work focuses on Stormwater Treatment Areas, the Corkscrew Regional Ecosystem Watershed, and nearby rivers and canals connected to waterways previously sampled. The interconnected canal and river network can help non-native and invasive species spread, which makes python distribution difficult to determine.According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the scientists used water samples to look for traces of python DNA and estimate where the snakes occur. The project examined possible waterways that could serve as corridors for northward expansion.How are scientists using eDNA to track Burmese pythonsUSGS scientists developed and optimised python-specific eDNA markers to detect Burmese pythons from water samples taken from southern Florida. The project surveyed Stormwater Treatment Areas (STAs), the Corkscrew Regional Ecosystem Watershed (CREW), and adjacent river or canal systems connected to previously sampled waterways. The aim was to improve understanding of where Burmese pythons are found across South Florida.The scientists used eDNA techniques to understand where the snakes occur and estimate their occurrence in the region. These estimates helped identify possible waterways that may be used as corridors for northward expansion. The work focused on waterways because southern Florida has an interconnected network of canals and rivers that can help non-native and invasive aquatic and semi-aquatic species, including Burmese pythons, spread across the region.How were water samples tested for Burmese pythonsWater samples were collected throughout five Stormwater Treatment Areas. Water samples were collected from canals at 38 sampling sites, as well as from lakes, ponds and reservoirs. The water was filtered to concentrate eDNA from the samples. Scientists then isolated the concentrated eDNA using optimised procedures designed to increase eDNA yield and reduce inhibitors such as tannins and humic acid, compounds characteristic of tea-coloured waters.To detect Burmese pythons, the researchers developed and optimised three species-specific markers, consisting of two primers and a fluorescently labelled probe. These markers were used on a droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) platform. According to USGS, ddPCR has higher accuracy and precision than quantitative PCR (qPCR) and can detect a single molecule of DNA from an environmental sample.Why detecting Burmese pythons through eDNA is challengingDetecting Burmese python eDNA is challenging because the snakes are semi-aquatic reptiles that shed limited amounts of DNA directly into water bodies. Low python densities can also result in lower eDNA concentrations. Southern Florida adds challenges, including large suspended sediment, high microbial communities, and environmental inhibitors in water samples.These conditions can make detection difficult and can limit the ability to draw conclusive information from negative results. Sampling design is important because weak sampling can lead to false-negative eDNA results. It should consider species density as well as differences in habitat and land use. According to USGS, adaptive sampling methods and estimates of occurrence and detection can increase confidence in both positive and negative eDNA results.Next steps for improving python detectionThe USGS says data from previous years will be used to refine sampling methods because expanding Burmese python populations may have low densities and low concentrations of snake eDNA. Accurate sampling of the region's water bodies can be difficult, and data collection will likely vary by habitat type. More sampling or alternative sampling locations throughout the study area may be needed to estimate Burmese python range delimitation. Limited water flow can also concentrate inhibitors in these areas. Many samples contained inhibitors even after extra removal processes. Ongoing efforts are focused on improving the removal of PCR inhibitors to support better data analysis. The project continues to refine detection methods for detecting Burmese pythons and estimating their distribution in southern Florida waterways.

articles.title: South Portland placed more than 200 discarded holiday trees on an eroded Maine beach after a 2022 storm; they trapped sand and vegetation began returning within months
articles.summary: After a powerful winter storm stripped away sections of Maine’s coastline in December 2022, an unlikely form of coastal protection began taking shape on
articles.body: After a powerful winter storm stripped away sections of Maine’s coastline in December 2022, an unlikely form of coastal protection began taking shape on the sand. Instead of sending discarded Christmas trees to waste facilities, South Portland put more than 200 of them to work along the damaged Willard Beach, where they were arranged to slow erosion and capture drifting sand, states a report by NOAA's Office for Coastal Management. The experiment was part of a broader effort led by the Maine Geological Survey, working with South Portland, Bristol and Phippsburg. Across three beaches, storm debris and unwanted holiday trees were repurposed as temporary structures to help rebuild dunes. Within months, vegetation began returning in some areas.Turning trees into dune buildersAccording to the report, the approach was straightforward: place woody material where dunes had been damaged and allow wind and waves to do much of the restoration work. At Willard Beach, the Christmas trees were positioned in rows parallel to the shoreline, roughly following the shape of natural dune ridges. Their branches helped slow moving sand, allowing it to accumulate rather than being carried away.The project was particularly important because erosion had exposed or threatened buried infrastructure along parts of the beach. A solid waste permit from the Maine Department of Environmental Protection helped make the reuse effort possible.As sand collected around the trees, the beach began developing conditions more favourable to the return of vegetation.Three beaches, three approachesThe wider project also examined how woody debris could be used in different coastal settings. At Pemaquid Beach in Bristol, the storm had carved steep, eroded faces into the dunes. Sections of washed-up logs were placed perpendicular to the shoreline to reinforce the base of the damaged dunes. Overhanging sections were allowed to collapse, helping accelerate the natural reshaping process.At Popham Beach State Park in Phippsburg, the storm had flattened large sections of the dunes and pushed the Morse River channel northward. Dozens of logs washed ashore were arranged parallel to the beach, creating lines that resembled natural dune ridges. The structures were intended to capture windblown sand and gradually rebuild the dunes. The work was carried out with the Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands.Letting nature do the restThe projects did not rely on elaborate construction or permanent barriers. Instead, the trees acted as rough, temporary sand traps while natural processes supplied the materials needed for recovery. Windblown sand became caught in branches and accumulated around the woody structures. Wave-deposited material added to the buildup in some areas, while returning vegetation helped stabilise newly formed sand.The results offered Maine officials another tool for responding to storm-damaged beaches, particularly where traditional engineering solutions may be costly or disruptive to natural dune systems.A second life for holiday treesThe projects also demonstrated how material that would normally be discarded can serve a practical purpose after the holiday season. In South Portland, more than 200 unwanted Christmas trees became part of an effort to protect a vulnerable stretch of shoreline. The work across Willard, Pemaquid and Popham beaches highlighted the value of combining local knowledge, government agencies and natural processes. Rather than trying to force eroded beaches back into their former shape, the projects gave sand, vegetation and dunes a framework in which to rebuild themselves.Image Courtesy: NOAA

articles.title: In 2022, he built a pocket-sized device to extract drinking water from the air in Death Valley using only sunlight; in 2025, he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry
articles.summary: Between August 19 and 23, 2022, Omar Yaghi's team placed a thermos-sized cylinder in Furnace Creek, inside the Death Valley National Park.
articles.body: Between August 19 and 23, 2022, Omar Yaghi's team placed a thermos-sized cylinder in Furnace Creek, inside the Death Valley National Park. The device was not connected to anything and for three complete cycles of night and day the device extracted liquid water from the air of one of the driest and hottest places on the planet. Two years later, Yaghi's invention scored him a Nobel Prize in Chemistry, the first to a Saudi national, according to a report by Vozpopuli.From humble beginnings to big solutionsOmar M. Yaghi was born in 1965 in Amman, Jordan, into a refugee family originally from Palestine. He grew up in a single room with his parents, eight siblings, and even livestock — a few cows. His father, who ran a butcher shop and raised cattle, insisted that his son pursue an education abroad. At 15, in 1980, with limited English, Yaghi moved alone to Troy, New York.He enrolled at Hudson Valley Community College shortly after arriving and then transferred to the State University of New York (SUNY) at Albany in 1983, where he developed a deep passion for chemistry. To support himself during this period, Yaghi bagged groceries and mopped floors. He graduated cum laude in 1985 with a Bachelor of Science in chemistry. Pursuing further specialisation, he earned a PhD in chemistry from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1990. Following his doctorate, Yaghi was awarded a prestigious National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellowship at Harvard University, where he worked from 1990 to 1992.By 1992, he secured a faculty position at Arizona State University, where he began shaping his career. In 1999, he joined the University of Michigan faculty, followed by a move to UCLA in 2007. In 2012, Yaghi joined the University of California, Berkeley, as a professor of chemistry. There, he became co-director of the Kavli Energy NanoScience Institute and served as Director of the Molecular Foundry at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory from 2012 to 2013. Today, Yaghi holds the James and Neeltje Tretter Chair in the College of Chemistry at UC Berkeley. He is the founding director of the Berkeley Global Science Institute, established to promote international scientific collaboration, and co-director of the California Research Alliance by BASF, focused on sustainable chemical research.The work for waterAs a child living in Jordan, Yaghi often queued up for water, an experience that inspired his work. “You store as much water as you can within those four hours and that’s the water you would use for those two weeks. If you ran out of water, you had to find a different source," Yaghi said in a documentary. “I grew up really appreciating the stress caused by water. It affects all aspects of life."The device Omar Yaghi used to extract water from the air in Death Valley contains 35 grams of a material called MOF-303, and what it produces each day, at the rate measured in the desert, fits in a spoonful. The figure used by the team at the University of California, Berkeley, is different: 210 grams of water per kilogram of material per day, about a glassful, and this is the figure that indicates the potential scale of the idea.“We have now shown that these materials, mounted on a device, can collect water from the air even in the most arduous and extreme conditions, including Death Valley,” explained Yaghi, the chemist who led the work, when presenting the results in 2023. The conditions were recorded in the article the team published in July 2023 in the journal Nature Water (available at this link ). The ground reached 65 degrees Celsius during the day, the average relative humidity at night remained at 14%, and the peak barely reached 21% around 4:30 a.m., which is when the device does its work.“MOFs are a completely new chemistry, based on joining inorganic and organic units in large porous structures,” summarises Yaghi, who invented this family of materials in the 1990s. The one inside the cylinder is called MOF-303; it contains aluminium and works like a sponge that absorbs moisture from the air at night and, during the day, with the sun's heat, releases it as vapour that condenses on the cold walls and drips into a reservoir.The 210 grams per kilo dropped to 114 on the driest night and rose to 285 in the control trial that the team repeated in Berkeley with much more pleasant humidity, and of all the vapour that the device captures, it returns between 85% and 90% as drinking water.Setting an exampleYaghi has never promoted the prototype as a consumer solution and defends it as proof that the principle works without an electric grid.On October 8, 2025, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry to three scientists: Omar Yaghi, Susumu Kitagawa of Kyoto University, and Richard Robson of the University of Melbourne. The trio was recognised "for the development of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs)," a class of materials that have revolutionised the ability to trap gases, capture carbon dioxide, and even harvest water from desert air.In February 2026, his company, Atoco, unveiled a machine that, according to the company, produces up to 1,000 litres per day using solar energy in air with less than 20% humidity, although that figure comes from the manufacturer and there is still no published trial to support it, like the one from Furnace Creek. “The science is already here; what’s needed now is the courage to scale these solutions,” Yaghi said at the presentation.

articles.title: Meet the world's smallest deer: The tiny ‘Pudu’ is barely four apples tall, weighs only a few kilograms and lives in South America's forests
articles.summary: This animal in photos may look more like a small forest mammal, more like a rabbit than a deer, but it is a real member of the deer family.
articles.body: This animal in photos may look more like a small forest mammal, more like a rabbit than a deer, but it is a real member of the deer family. It is a ‘pudu,’ a group of two deer species found in South America and known for their exceptionally small size. The northern pudu (Pudu mephistophiles) can stand only about 32 to 35 cm at the shoulder and weigh roughly 3.3 to 6 kg. That makes the “four apples tall” description a striking visual way to understand its size, although the exact height of four apples naturally varies with the size of the apples. Guinness World Records lists the northern pudu as the smallest deer species, with a maximum shoulder height of 35 cm and weight of up to 6 kg.The smallest of the deerPudus belong to the deer family, Cervidae, so despite their unusually small size, they are not a separate type of miniature animal. There are two recognised species commonly referred to as pudus: the northern pudu and the southern pudu. The northern pudu is the smaller of the two. It is found in the Andes of Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, generally in high-elevation habitats. Sources on the species describe it as occurring at elevations of roughly 2,000 to 4,000 metres, including montane forests and high-altitude habitats.The southern pudu (Pudu puda) is larger. It is native to southern Chile and southwestern Argentina, where it lives in temperate forests and areas with dense understory vegetation. Adult southern pudus generally stand about 35 to 45 cm at the shoulder and weigh around 6.5 to 13.5 kg, according to the Animal Diversity Web.Small body, very different habitatThe pudu's compact size is suited to the thick vegetation of its forest habitat. Southern pudus, for example, are associated with dense understory containing shrubs, small trees and bamboo-like vegetation. They can use narrow trails through the undergrowth and move through forest areas where a larger deer would have more difficulty. According to the Los Angeles Zoo, pudus are active mainly around dawn and dusk and they can move through forest undergrowth, climb over fallen trees and stand on their hind legs to reach leaves or fruit. When threatened, they may run in a zig-zag pattern or remain still in an attempt to avoid detection.Yes, they have antlersTheir size does not mean they have lost the features associated with deer. Male pudus grow antlers, although these are tiny compared with those of many other deer species. In southern pudus, the antlers are generally only about 6 to 9 cm long, while northern pudu males have antlers of about 6 cm. Females do not grow antlers. The southern pudu also shows another familiar deer feature during its early life. Young animals have lighter spots on their backs, which disappear as they grow. According to the Animal Diversity Web, these spots are generally lost by around eight weeks of age.The other pudu is still remarkably smallEven though the southern pudu is larger than its northern relative, it remains exceptionally small for a deer. The Animal Diversity Web describes it as the second-smallest deer in the world, with adults generally reaching 35–45 cm at the shoulder. Pudus are also known for being elusive. Their dense forest habitat makes them difficult to observe, while their small bodies and ability to move through thick vegetation help them stay out of sight. Their predators include pumas, foxes, wild cats, dogs and owls.
tags: smallest deer species in the world

articles.title: Volunteers at a protected Cape Cod nesting site found a rare diamondback terrapin hatchling with two heads; the tiny turtle weighed about as much as a nickel and is now being monitored by wildlife veterinarians
articles.summary: A tiny diamondback terrapin has become an unexpected discovery on Cape Cod after volunteers found a hatchling with two heads at a protected nesting site
articles.body: A tiny diamondback terrapin has become an unexpected discovery on Cape Cod after volunteers found a hatchling with two heads at a protected nesting site in Wellfleet, Massachusetts. According to Mass Audubon’s Wellfleet Bay Wildlife Sanctuary, the unusual hatchling was one of the surprises during the sanctuary’s terrapin nesting season and was taken to a licensed wildlife rehabilitation facility for care and monitoring. The 5.2-gram turtle has a rare developmental condition called bicephaly, according to the Cape Wildlife Center. Veterinarians are now watching its appetite, growth, behaviour and development while they learn more about how its two heads and body function together.An unusual discovery during nesting seasonThe two-headed turtle was found during the annual diamondback terrapin conservation work at Wellfleet Bay. For years, volunteers have spent the nesting season searching for terrapins, locating their nests and protecting the eggs from predators. The work is particularly important on Cape Cod because the diamondback terrapin is listed as threatened in Massachusetts. The species lives in brackish environments, where salt water and fresh water meet, and females come onto land during the summer to lay their eggs in sandy areas above the high-tide line.Mass Audubon's Wellfleet Bay programme has been protecting terrapin nests since 2005. During the 2024 nesting season alone, more than 125 volunteers worked across nine locations in Wellfleet, Eastham and Orleans, protecting more than 200 nests on sanctuary property. The unusual two-headed hatchling was discovered during this wider conservation effort.The tiny turtle weighs just 5.2 gramsThe hatchling is remarkably small. When it arrived at the Cape Wildlife Center in Barnstable on September 17, 2026, it weighed 5.2 grams, roughly the weight of a nickel. Despite its unusual appearance, the turtle has been showing encouraging signs. The veterinary team reported that both heads are alert and that the hatchling has been eating and behaving normally.The condition responsible for its unusual appearance is called bicephaly. It is a rare developmental abnormality in which an embryo develops with two heads rather than separating completely into two individuals. The exact internal anatomy of this particular turtle is still unknown. As it grows, veterinarians expect to be able to use diagnostic imaging such as X-rays and CT scans to better understand how its internal organs and body structures are arranged. For now, the priority is much simpler: keep the tiny animal healthy and watch how it develops.A rare case even for experienced wildlife rescuersTwo-headed animals are extremely unusual, but this is not the first time wildlife specialists on Cape Cod have encountered one. Mass Audubon’s Wellfleet Bay Wildlife Sanctuary described the discovery of a two-headed diamondback terrapin as one of only a few such cases recorded during the programme's nearly five-decade history. The Cape Wildlife Center has also cared for other bicephalic terrapins in recent years. That experience means the current hatchling is being watched by a team that has encountered similar developmental abnormalities before. Still, every animal can be different, and veterinarians are waiting to learn how this particular turtle develops. The centre has said that cases like this provide an opportunity to learn more about the anatomy and physiology of these unusual animals.Why protecting these turtles mattersThe discovery comes against the backdrop of a much larger conservation effort. Diamondback terrapins spend most of their lives in narrow strips of salt marsh, while females move onto land to nest. Their eggs and hatchlings face threats from predators including foxes, raccoons and skunks. Roads are another danger, particularly for adult females crossing to nesting areas. Habitat loss, coastal development and the wildlife pet trade also put pressure on populations.Climate change adds another challenge. Mass Audubon’s Wellfleet Bay Wildlife Sanctuary has noted that rising sea levels and unusually high tides can alter traditional nesting areas. During the 2024 season, for example, winter storms pushed a high-tide line farther into one of the sanctuary's traditional nesting areas, prompting more females to look for alternative sites. Volunteers therefore play a major role in helping the turtles reach adulthood. They patrol nesting areas, look for tracks and nests, install protective cages and monitor hatchlings. In 2024, the sanctuary recorded 4,810 terrapin hatchlings released after 82% of eggs in protected nests survived.What happens to the two-headed terrapin now?For the unusual hatchling, the next stage is simply continued observation. Veterinarians are monitoring its appetite, growth, behaviour and development while they learn more about how its two heads and body function together. Its sex cannot yet be determined, and its long-term future remains uncertain. If the turtle grows strong enough to survive independently, wildlife experts could eventually consider whether it can return to the wild. If its condition prevents that, it may instead remain in human care. For now, the tiny terrapin represents both an unusual scientific opportunity and another reminder of the work involved in protecting Cape Cod's threatened turtle population.What began as another nesting-season patrol ended with volunteers finding an animal few people ever get to see: a 5.2-gram diamondback terrapin with two heads. While its future is still unknown, the fact that it was found, rescued and placed under veterinary care gives the hatchling a chance to grow while experts learn more about this exceptionally rare condition.
tags: Mass Audubon’s Wellfleet Bay Wildlife Sanctuary

articles.title: Powerful 'Kelvin wave' triggered by super El Niño threatens to raise sea levels off the California coast for months
articles.summary: A disturbance characterized by above-normal sea levels is spreading up the Pacific coast of Central and North America, and it could make the damage from pred...
articles.body:
A powerful "Kelvin" wave triggered by this year's super El Nino is creeping up the Pacific coast of Central and North America, raising sea levels by up to 1 foot for months.

Internal Kelvin waves, generated during El Nino years, cause oscillations of a boundary within the ocean as well as a height increase at the surface, amplifying the damage from severe storms, storm surges, flooding, and coastal erosion.

California and other regions bordering the eastern Pacific Ocean are vulnerable to the influence of internal Kelvin waves, which distort normal tides and tidal currents, causing tides to rise by "tens of centimeters" or about a foot, magnifying the impacts of storms.

A powerful "Kelvin wave," triggered by this year's super El Niño , is creeping up the Pacific coast of Central and North America and will soon reach California's shores, where it could raise sea levels by up to 1 foot (30 centimeters) for months, researchers warn.

Kelvin waves are a well-known, planetary-scale ocean phenomenon, but this particular forecast has experts worried because it will likely amplify the damage from severe storms, storm surges, flooding and coastal erosion that the record-shattering El Niño is expected to bring this winter .

In general, a Kelvin wave is a swell wave that spans thousands of miles and balances Earth's rotation, David Webb , a physical oceanographer at the National Oceanography Centre in the U.K., told Live Science in an email. But the waves generated during El Niño years are not normal Kelvin waves, because they cause oscillations of a boundary within the ocean as well as a height increase at the surface. In particular, these waves trigger the border between warmer, less-dense surface water and colder, denser bottom layers to move up and down within about 330 feet (100 m). For this reason, these El Niño-driven waves are called internal Kelvin waves.

Internal Kelvin waves are triggered by changes in surface winds around the equator in the far-western Pacific Ocean. Specifically, westerly wind bursts weaken the background trade winds that blow from South America toward Asia, thereby allowing warm water and elevated sea states that occur in the far-western Pacific to slowly "slosh" eastward.

In this case, "the generation process will have involved changes in the winds at different locations and at different times, so it may not be a particularly clean single wave — possibly a bit messy," Webb said.

Once an internal Kelvin wave kicks off, researchers can track its advance along the equator and predict when it will hit the South American coastline. The wave can't go farther east than that, so it spreads into two branches — known as coastal trapped waves — that continue north and south for thousands of miles at a speed of around 6 mph (10 km/h) . This means California is not uniquely exposed to the current wave; all of the countries and regions that border the eastern Pacific Ocean are vulnerable, Webb said.

In California and elsewhere, the influence of the internal Kelvin wave will be in addition to the tides, regardless of whether El Niño sparks storm activity there. "What is most likely to be seen is a period, or maybe a few weeks, when the normal [pattern] of tides and tidal currents is distorted, with both high and low tides being higher than normal," Webb said, adding that tides could rise by "tens of centimeters," or about a foot.

The problem is that higher tides magnify the impacts of storms, which are more likely in some parts of the U.S. during an El Niño, Kate Huckelbridge , executive director of the California Coastal Commission, wrote in a Sept. 11 memo . The memo was sent to warn coastal California homeowners and residents to prepare for extreme conditions, such as flooding.

"A key observation from past El Niño events is that the most damaging storms are often those that coincide with the highest tides," Huckelbridge wrote. "Storms that peak during high tides are far more likely to cause damage than if the same storm peaked during low tide."

Storms alone can raise coastal sea levels by more than 3 feet (1 m), Webb noted, and sea levels have already increased by at least 8 inches (20 cm) due to climate change . Last week, California Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a state of emergency in response to experts' weather predictions so the state could mobilize equipment and resources before storms strike, The Guardian reported Monday (Sept. 28).

Several internal Kelvin waves can occur within a single El Niño event, with the largest waves typically recorded in the winter. However, Webb said he doubts there will be more than one full wave this time.

A Kelvin wave is a disturbance characterized by higher-than-normal sea levels. Here, we see one hitting the northern tip of South America and propagating northward. | Credit: Dillon Amaya/North Carolina State University

articles.title: This blog could help you poop better
articles.summary: This week’s Optimizer tackles the recent fibermaxxing trend. While it does raise awareness of an underconsumed nutrient, not all fiber is created equal.
articles.body: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here. “I will explode your butthole with this poopmaxxer pesto,” a calm Gen Z voice announced from my phone’s speakers. “And don’t worry, it doesn’t taste like poop, unless that’s what you’re into … I don’t know if Italians will approve of this, but it’s for my … a-butt-a-hole-a!” What followed in that video was actually a pretty good recipe. Two cups of blanched peas mixed into a fairly standard pesto recipe for a yield of 18 grams of fiber. Never mind my spouse’s flabbergasted face as the video played over and over while I blanched and blended in the kitchen. Not all TikTok fibermaxxers are as disturbingly whimsical as @hallysicle, a self-described “chaotic wellness” creator responsible for the poopmaxxer pesto; the cognitive dissonance of her deadpan scatological narration, cottagecore kawaii aesthetic, and actually good recipes is very much her own creation. That said, many of TikTok’s fiberheads are gleefully unhinged when preaching the benefits of the criminally underappreciated and underconsumed macronutrient. There’s Liam, a friendly nutritional fad debunker who’s also gained fame as “the Bean Guy” for his love of beans and fiber. He is regularly summoned in the comments of any bean recipe. (Once showing up as an actual ghostly beanfather.) On the other side of the spectrum, there’s Fiber Daddy — a dry influencer who says you’re being “a total dumdum” for throwing away your broccoli stems. He claims to poop four times daily and sells a supplement called Liquid Salad. But perhaps more surprising are the fiber-obsessed healthcare providers also jumping in on the trend. [Media: Considering that roughly 95 percent of Americans fall short of the daily recommended amount of fiber, you’d think fibermaxxing is unequivocally a good thing. But as with anything on the internet, “maxxing” doesn’t always tell the whole story. Why is the internet suddenly obsessed with fiber and pooping? There’s no single reason, but rather a few larger-scale health trends converging with the influencer content economy. Take GLP-1 usage. The so-called Ozempic economy is one big reason why you’re seeing a huge push for fresh foods and proteinwashing at the grocery store. Because GLP-1s can suppress appetite, people on these medications have to prioritize protein and fiber in their diets to prevent muscle loss and alleviate gastrointestinal side effects. (One example: those Grüns gummy bears appealing to GLP-1 users in their marketing.) This affects an increasingly large portion of the population. A recent Gallup survey has found that in the US, GLP-1 usage has skyrocketed to 11 percent in 2026 from 3 percent just two years ago. There’s also been a rising number of videos featuring young people in their 20s and 30s sharing their stories of battling colon cancer. These videos are often bolstered by social media-savvy gastroenterologists and dietitians who are also trying to raise awareness of this trend and early-onset symptoms. There are likely several reasons why colorectal cancer is on the rise, but one common refrain: Partaking in a fiber-rich diet can help reduce risk compared to the typical American diet. [Image: Beans beans the magical fruit, the more you eat the more you toot, because they’re a good source of fiber. The scary thing is that this isn’t baseless fearmongering or a viral trend taking science out of context. A recent study has found that mortality from colorectal cancer in people under 50 has been increasing by 1.1 percent per year since 2005, making it the leading cause of cancer-related death in this cohort. Today, the American Cancer Society estimates that 45 percent of new diagnoses come from people under 65 years old, a significant increase from 27 percent in 1995. So all things considered, yes — fiber (and therefore, pooping) is on a lot of people’s minds. That, in turn, makes it ripe for contentmaxxing online. In some respects, this could be a good thing. While RFK Jr.’s MAHA movement has zeroed in on protein — a nutrient that the vast majority of Americans are not deficient in — fiber is an important and consequential macronutrient that virtually everyone gets too little of. Put plainly, dietary fiber is a type of complex carbohydrate that the body can’t digest and primarily comes from plant foods. It also comes in two types: soluble and insoluble. The former dissolves in water, forming a gel-like substance in your gut that helps lower cholesterol and blood glucose levels. The latter helps add bulk to your poops, making them easier to pass and helps prevent constipation. On top of these benefits, a high-fiber diet is associated with greater satiety — good for weight management — and overall bowel health by helping prevent hemorrhoids, feeding the beneficial bacteria in your gut microbiome, and, again, reducing overall colorectal cancer risk. But as with any health trend, more is not always better. Not all fiber is created equal. To be fair, the majority of fibermaxxers online tend to focus on fiber-rich diets featuring whole foods. Inspiration for palatable ways to sneak in veggies, oats, beans, or leafy greens during busy weeks, sometimes in quirky ways. That kind of fibermaxxing content is relatively harmless. You just might hear a lot about poop and see numerous poop emojis. But social media often erases nuance to sell you something. And it’s only a matter of time before companies hawking fiber supplements hop on the bandwagon. Three supplements I’ve previously covered in Optimizer are already doing this. There’s AG1, which has a whole fiber page to promote its Essentials Gummies product. (It’s more famous greens powder only has 2g of fiber, after all.) Huel, a meal replacement drink, sells a fiber boost bundle. And then there’s the aforementioned Grüns, which prominently features its 6g of fiber per pack in its marketing. Considering how the commercial food industry is stuffing protein into every product, it wouldn’t take much for fibermaxxed versions of ultra-processed foods to start hitting shelves — if they haven’t already. [Image: Sometimes I hate being right. As part of a diverse diet, fiber supplements aren’t the worst thing. The problem is you need both soluble and insoluble fiber in your diet to get all the benefits. Supplements tend to overindex on inulin, psyllium husk, or tapioca fiber — all of which are soluble and, in excess, can cause a lot of gas. (Turns out, a soluble source is generally easier to incorporate into various forms.) Fiber supplements have their time and place! But it’s also in the name. They’re meant to supplement in a pinch, not be the convenient way to get fiber while avoiding plants in your diet. Speaking of gas, some fibermaxxers are actually advocating for fartmaxxing with absurd goals like 60 to 100g of fiber per day. Technically, there is no official upper limit to fiber. The unofficial limit is what your digestive system can handle. Just as a diet full of diverse fiber sources can alleviate gas and bloating, going ham on fiber intake too quickly can cause gastrointestinal distress. (Beans have a reputation for a reason.) The daily recommended amount of fiber is roughly 14 grams per 1,000 calories — or 25 to 38g per day depending on age and caloric needs. Health experts and the literature largely agree that’s what most people should aspire to, slowly, gradually, and with lots of water to mitigate negative side effects until the digestive system adjusts. Lastly, not everyone can boost their fiber intake willy-nilly. Those with Crohn’s disease, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, or bowel obstructions need to consult their doctors. The same goes for people on certain thyroid, cardiovascular, diabetes, and depression medications. Fiber supplements, for example, can interfere with absorption and make a drug less effective, so meal timing becomes more important. [Image: Conversely, while these are poo-shaped macaroons, the fiber content is likely very low. Of all the “maxxing” trends, fibermaxxing has been one of the less problematic. (So far.) Most dietitians and gastroenterologists would likely rejoice if more people strolled into their appointments asking for help in boosting fiber intake. But in the wellness wild west, things can get stupid real fast. Part of why maxxing hits so hard with health trends is that it taps into fearmongering — often about genuine concerns based on a modicum of science — with an easy black-and-white solution. Social media creators, including well-intentioned ones, hop onto sound bites to gain views, and then affiliate partnership deals to keep the lights on. Nuance is tragically less viral. The truth is, doctors have been telling us all to prioritize fiber for decades. Eat the rainbow. Prioritize whole foods. Make sure to eat a serving of veggies with each meal. Whole grains over refined grains! All of these could be considered the OG fibermaxxing commandments. They’ll also still be true once the fibermaxxing moment has given way to the next eye-searing, brain-breaking health fad.

articles.title: Boeing’s Starliner set for uncrewed test flight in December
articles.summary: Starliner’s first crewed test flight left two astronauts stranded on the ISS for nine months.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — NASA is planning an uncrewed test flight of Boeing’s troubled Starliner capsule for the end of the year, pushing ahead with the project after a failed crewed test flight.

NASA administrator Jared Isaacman announced Monday that NASA would be putting extra money and support behind the project after its “ Type A mishap ,” a designation used for the most severe problems.

An improved Starliner is set to launch no earlier than December, carrying cargo on an uncrewed mission to the International Space Station.

Astronauts are not expected to fly on the capsule until 2028, with safety redesigns expected to take months or years to complete. Astronaut Woody Hoburg is set to command the mission, though NASA has not released information on his crewmates.

Starliner’s first crewed mission fell apart after astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams found their eight-to-10-day ISS stay extended to nine months .

After experiencing issues with helium leaks and the failure of five reaction control system thrusters , Starliner made it safely to the ISS with its crew.

However, NASA deemed the capsule unsafe to ferry its crew back home, eventually jettisoning Starliner for an unpiloted trip back to Earth and developing an alternate plan to bring Williams and Wilmore back to Earth.

The two astronauts eventually made their way home on a SpaceX Dragon capsule , leaving Starliner grounded while NASA and Boeing attempted to determine what went wrong.

Planned repairs to Starliner include replacing seals to prevent helium leaks and developing a process to prevent corrosion on the RCS thrusters that caused some of them to fail.

NASA’s goal was to have two U.S.-based ways to transport astronauts to and from the ISS, but Starliner’s woes made the agency reliant on SpaceX, which the company is set to phase out by 2030.

The ISS itself is currently set to be abandoned by 2031 , though private U.S. companies are working on orbital stations that would need reliable transport for occupants.

Fixing Starliner will cost NASA $359 million, but would give the agency a new crew vehicle option as SpaceX pivots to Starship , which is too large for traditional docking stations, and shifts focus to Mars travel as a primary goal.

articles.title: A London museum's urban garden collected more than 11 million environmental records in one year; 50 sensors tracked heat, birdsong and underwater sounds
articles.summary: A garden at London’s Natural History Museum has collected more than 11 million environmental data records during its first year as a high-tech living
articles.body: A garden at London’s Natural History Museum has collected more than 11 million environmental data records during its first year as a high-tech living laboratory. More than 50 sensors now monitor conditions across the Nature Discovery Garden, recording everything from temperature and humidity to birdsong, underwater sounds and traffic noise. The information is being gathered continuously and stored through a new data system built with Amazon Web Services technology. The project is giving researchers a detailed way to study how wildlife and urban environments interact in one of London’s busiest areas.How are 11 million environmental records being collected in the gardenThe Nature Discovery Garden is part of the Natural History Museum’s transformed 5-acre outdoor space in South Kensington. It opened to the public in July 2024, and the sensor network, which was completed in September 2025, has since turned the garden into what the museum describes as a living laboratory.According to the Natural History Museum, more than 50 sensors are now operating across the gardens. They collect real-time information about the environment, including temperature and humidity, while acoustic equipment records sounds from the pond, bird calls and background urban noise such as traffic. The museum published the 11-million-record figure in August 2026, marking the first year of data collection through the network.The Amazon Web Services account of the project described a network of 25 sensors when the system was completed in September 2025. That system was designed to collect environmental sounds as well as other measurements, with the audio network expected to gather up to 20 terabytes of data during its first year.What can the sensors reveal about urban natureThe measurements allow researchers to see changes that might otherwise be difficult to notice during an ordinary visit to the garden. Temperature and humidity readings can show how conditions vary between different parts of the site, while sound recordings provide another way of tracking wildlife and activity.The Natural History Museum says the information can help scientists understand how nature responds to pressures in an urban setting. The recordings include underwater sounds from the pond as well as birdsong and city noise, creating a picture that goes beyond simply counting the species present.The EDP24 report, published when the sensors were switched on in September 2025, highlighted that the researchers would use the live information to study wildlife ranging from insects and frogs to microscopic organisms.Centralised data collection facility by AmazonThe large amount of information is fed into the Natural History Museum’s Data Ecosystem, which was developed using AWS cloud technology. Instead of keeping different research datasets separate, the system allows observations from sensors, images and other scientific sources to be collected and processed in one place.Amazon Web Services says the platform was created to give museum scientists a central way to securely store and work with research data. It can also expand as more information is collected, allowing researchers working on different urban biodiversity projects to use the same system.The museum is also adding information from community science programmes. According to Amazon, the Data Ecosystem had already received 156 audio recordings from the Nature Overheard programme and more than 57,000 visual wildlife observations from historic museum garden records dating back to 1995 by July 2024.How the garden is showing the effects of urban heatOne of the clearest uses of the new sensor network has come from studying urban heat. During a heatwave in June, soil temperature sensors in the woodland areas of the museum gardens recorded temperatures 10°C lower than those in paved areas of the Darwin Centre Courtyard.The Natural History Museum says these measurements can help researchers examine how different urban environments respond to rising temperatures. The work is also being used to explore how features such as trees, shade, soil moisture and surfaces that allow water to pass through can influence cooling.Rather than relying only on observations made during occasional research visits, the sensors can provide measurements over time. This gives scientists a way to compare different parts of the garden and examine how planting and surrounding surfaces affect local conditions.Importance of London’s garden for long-term wildlife researchThe sensor project is based on decades of observations from the museum’s gardens. The Natural History Museum says monitoring carried out since 1995 has recorded more than 3,500 species using the garden, with the blackbird the most frequently observed species.Since the garden reopened in 2024, researchers have identified another 90 species that had not previously been recorded there. Among them are the Emperor Moth and Small Red-Eyed Damselfly.The garden is also being used to study the effects of conservation work. One current project is examining what happened after material from the pond in the former Wildlife Garden was moved into the Nature Discovery Garden, allowing researchers to investigate the wider effects of that intervention on the garden ecosystem.The monitoring project is not staying within the Nature Discovery Garden. The Natural History Museum says the sensor network is now being expanded into its Evolution Garden, where visitor numbers are higher and the planting style is different.That expansion could allow researchers to compare how visitor activity and different habitat designs affect biodiversity. For a garden surrounded by one of London’s busiest urban areas, the project provides a way to study nature at a much finer level.

articles.title: Álvaro Puche, entrenador personal: “El principal error que cometen las mujeres de 60 años al salir a caminar es el de darle mayor importancia al tiempo que a la intensidad"
articles.standfirst: El preparador físico da las claves para aprovechar al máximo los beneficios de caminar
articles.summary: El preparador físico da las claves para aprovechar al máximo los beneficios de caminar
articles.body: Salir a caminar es uno de los deportes más tranquilos y a la vez más beneficiosos para la salud que cualquier persona puede practicar. En los últimos años ha crecido la tendencia y la información sobre los beneficios de completar los 10.000 pasos diarios que puede registrar hasta nuestro propio teléfono. El entrenador personal, Álvaro Puche, ha comentado que al caminar es cuando más fácil es que cometamos errores. El especialista ha escrito varios libros en los que informa y comparte consejos para el entrenamiento de fuerza en personas de más de 60 años de edad. En una entrevista realizada hace un tiempo, Puche comenta que “El principal error que cometen las mujeres de 60 años cuando salen a caminar es el de darle mayor importancia al tiempo que están caminando que a la intensidad a la que lo están haciendo”. La realidad es que caminar a una intensidad alta es muy beneficioso para la salud, pero el preparador no se olvida de la importancia de realizar ejercicios en los que se involucre el empleo de fuerza física. Además, explica cómo se debe de caminar correctamente para aprovechar cada paso al máximo: “A un ritmo al que resultaría complicado pronunciar más de tres palabras seguidas si durante esta marcha a pie se quisiera mantener una conversación”. La razón es que cuanto más rápido caminemos más subirán las pulsaciones y, por tanto, mayor será el beneficio cardiovascular y más calorías quemaremos. En conclusión, caminar es el mejor complemento para el entrenamiento de fuerza, el cual es recomendable de realizar entre 3 y 4 veces por semana. De esta forma, el entrenamiento de fuerza ayudará a mantener la musculación, la resistencia y la movilidad, mientras que caminar aportará resistencia cardiovascular.
