articles.title: In the late 1950s and early 1960s, Nile perch were introduced into Lake Victoria to improve fisheries; decades later the predator was linked to the loss of many native cichlids and transformation of the lake’s fishery
articles.summary: In the late 1950s and early 1960s, Nile perch were introduced into Lake Victoria with the hope that the large predatory fish would strengthen local
articles.body: In the late 1950s and early 1960s, Nile perch were introduced into Lake Victoria with the hope that the large predatory fish would strengthen local fisheries. The decision was intended to create new commercial opportunities and increase the supply of valuable fish. Instead, the species spread through one of the world’s largest freshwater ecosystems and became linked to a dramatic decline in native fish. TheNational Invasive Species Information Center says Nile perch were introduced to Lake Victoria in 1954 and later destroyed about 200 native fish species through predation and competition for food. The story has become a powerful example of how a well-intentioned fisheries decision can produce consequences that extend far beyond its original goal.Why Nile perch were introducedLake Victoria, shared by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, has long supported communities that depend on fishing for food, income and trade. Before the arrival of Nile perch, the lake contained a remarkable variety of native fish, especially cichlids.Cichlids are a diverse group of freshwater fish known for their unusual variety of body shapes, feeding habits and behaviours. Lake Victoria was home to hundreds of native cichlid species, many of which had evolved within the lake and occupied highly specialised ecological roles.The Nile perch, scientifically known as Lates niloticus, is native to parts of Africa. It is a large freshwater predator that can grow much bigger than many of the fish already living in Lake Victoria. Fisheries managers believed that introducing it could create a commercially valuable fishery and provide a new source of income for lakeside communities.The introduction was not immediately understood as an ecological experiment of enormous scale. At the time, the focus was largely on increasing catches and improving the economic potential of the lake. The long-term effects of adding a powerful predator to a complex ecosystem were much harder to predict.A predator enters a complex food webNile perch did not simply become another fish in the lake. As predators, they competed with native species for food and consumed smaller fish. Their presence added new pressure to an ecosystem in which many species had developed alongside one another over thousands or millions of years.Native cichlids were particularly vulnerable because they occupied many of the lake’s feeding and habitat niches. Some ate algae, while others fed on insects, molluscs or smaller fish. The arrival of Nile perch introduced a predator capable of feeding on numerous species across different parts of the food web.The National Invasive Species Information Center reports that the species ultimately destroyed about 200 native fish species through predation and competition for food. The number illustrates the scale of the change, although scientists have also examined other factors that contributed to the decline of native fish, including overfishing, pollution, habitat changes and shifts in water quality.As the Nile perch population expanded, the balance of the fishery changed. A lake once known for its extraordinary variety of native fish increasingly became associated with a smaller number of commercially important species.The collapse of native cichlidsThe decline of Lake Victoria’s cichlids is one of the most widely discussed examples of biodiversity loss in a freshwater ecosystem. Many species disappeared from parts of the lake, while others became extremely rare or survived only in limited habitats.The loss was significant because the cichlids were not interchangeable. Each species had its own role in the ecosystem. Some were used to control algae, some to process nutrients, and some were prey for larger animals. When many species vanished, the lake lost not only individual fish but also the ecological functions they performed.The loss of native fish also affected the scientific knowledge. The cichlids of Lake Victoria, for example, diversified rapidly, evolving into related species with different traits and lifestyles. Their decline reduced the living diversity available for researchers studying evolution and adaptation.The change presented challenges and opportunities for local communities. Processing plants and exports were a large component of the Nile perch industry. At the same time, dependence on a smaller number of fish species made the fishery more vulnerable to changes in population, markets and environmental conditions.An economic success with environmental costsThe Nile perch fishery generated substantial economic activity around Lake Victoria. Large fish could be processed, transported and sold in domestic and international markets. In some areas, the new fishery provided jobs and income that the earlier, more diverse fishery had not produced at the same commercial scale.However, economic gains did not erase the environmental costs. Commercial Nile perch fishing was usually different in terms of equipment and techniques from traditional fishing. Some communities faced changes in access to fish, rising pressure on stocks and concerns about how profits were distributed.The fish also changed what people ate locally. Larger Nile perch were frequently directed towards commercial markets, while smaller or less valuable fish had previously formed an important part of local diets. In some lakeside communities, this raised concerns about food security and the affordability of fish.The experience showed that a species can be commercially valuable and ecologically disruptive at the same time. To simply label the introduction a success or failure would overlook the differential effects on various groups.Invasive species lessonsThe Lake Victoria case is frequently cited as an example of the perils of introducing non-native species. Even when an introduced animal appears likely to improve food production or create jobs, its effects can be difficult to contain once it becomes established.The National Invasive Species Information Center notes that preventing the introduction of harmful species is the most effective way to avoid their impacts. Once a predator has spread through a large and interconnected ecosystem, removing it can be extremely difficult, expensive and damaging in its own way.The Nile perch story also demonstrates why environmental decisions require more than short-term economic calculations. Assessments should include native biodiversity, food-webs, local livelihoods and the potential for an introduced species to alter the whole structure of an ecosystem.Lake Victoria has not been changed by Nile perch alone. Pollution, excessive fishing, invasive plants, shoreline development and climate-related pressures have also affected the lake. Yet the introduction remains one of the clearest examples of how a single management decision can reshape a vast natural system.A warning from one of the world’s great lakesThe Nile perch was introduced with the expectation that it would improve fisheries. Instead, it became a dominant predator linked to the loss of many native cichlids and the transformation of Lake Victoria’s fishery.The episode continues to influence discussions about conservation, fisheries management and invasive species control. It reminds policymakers that ecosystems are not empty spaces waiting for a more profitable species. They are networks of relationships and change one thing, change everything connected to it.For Lake Victoria, the legacy of the Nile perch is complicated. The fish created an important commercial industry, but it also helped drive one of the most dramatic freshwater biodiversity losses ever recorded. The lasting lesson is that improving a fishery cannot be measured only by the size of the catch. It must also account for what disappears when a new species takes over.

articles.title: In 1984, a $57 million gift from David and Lucile Packard helped open Monterey Bay Aquarium; its sea otter programme has since cared for over 1,000 stranded animals and surrogate-raised 84 pups
articles.summary: In 1984, a $57 million gift from David and Lucile Packard helped turn a former cannery site on California’s Cannery Row into the Monterey Bay Aquarium.
articles.body: In 1984, a $57 million gift from David and Lucile Packard helped turn a former cannery site on California’s Cannery Row into the Monterey Bay Aquarium. Four decades later, the institution is known not only for its kelp forest, jellyfish and deep-sea exhibits, but also for conservation work that reaches far beyond its walls. According to the David and Lucile Packard Foundation, the aquarium has welcomed more than 70 million visitors and developed major programmes in marine science and education. Its Sea Otter Recovery Program has cared for more than 1,000 stranded sea otters and successfully surrogate-raised 84 pups for release into the wild. Read on to know more about it here:A vision shaped by Monterey BayThe idea for the aquarium emerged from a group of people who believed Monterey Bay deserved greater public attention. Nancy Burnett, David Packard’s daughter, and her sister Julie Packard were among those who helped develop the vision after discussions with scientists working in the region.The project took six years of planning and a major financial commitment from David and Lucile Packard. Their $57 million gift helped make it possible to build a major public aquarium directly beside one of the most biologically rich marine environments in the world.The Monterey Bay Aquarium opened on October 20, 1984, on the site of a former sardine and squid cannery. The location was meaningful because Cannery Row had once been the centre of a major fishing industry before declining fish populations and economic pressures led to the closure of the last cannery in 1973.Rather than creating a general-purpose collection of marine animals, the aquarium focused on the species and habitats found along California’s Central Coast. It became the first major public aquarium with permanent exhibits devoted to the marine life of its local waters.Exhibits designed to inspire actionThe aquarium’s exhibits were created to give visitors a close look at habitats that many people could not easily explore for themselves. Its living kelp forest became one of the institution’s signature features, showing how an underwater ecosystem changes with light, currents, predators and plant growth. The aquarium also became known for its large-scale jellyfish exhibits and for its work with animals that are difficult to maintain in captivity. It was the first institution to successfully exhibit young great white sharks and return them to the ocean.These displays were not intended only to entertain. They helped visitors understand that ocean animals are connected through food webs and shared habitats. A kelp forest, for example, is not simply a collection of plants. It supports fish, invertebrates, sea otters and countless smaller organisms. The aquarium’s public education work also helped build interest in protecting the bay. In 1992, Monterey Bay became part of the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, which the Packard Foundation describes as the largest national marine sanctuary in the continental United States.From public aquarium to research leaderSoon after the aquarium opened, David Packard established the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, known as MBARI. The institute became a centre for ocean science and technology, developing underwater robots and other tools to study remote parts of the ocean. MBARI scientists, engineers and marine operations teams have explored areas that are difficult or impossible for divers to reach. Their work has helped expand knowledge of the seafloor and contributed to the discovery of hundreds of new species.The aquarium and MBARI have different roles, but their work is closely connected. MBARI produces scientific information and technology, while the aquarium helps translate complex discoveries into exhibitions, programmes and public conversations about the ocean. This combination gives the aquarium influence beyond its exhibits. Its work includes research, education, policy advocacy and conservation programmes focused on threatened species and damaged habitats.A second chance for stranded sea ottersThe Sea Otter Recovery Program has worked with southern sea otters for more than 40 years. The animals remain vulnerable to shark bites, disease, pollution, habitat loss and changes in the availability of prey. When an orphaned or stranded pup is found, the aquarium’s team responds and, when possible, attempts to reunite it with its mother. If that is not possible, the pup receives intensive care from specialists who limit human contact to prevent the animal from becoming accustomed to people.The aquarium then uses a distinctive surrogate-mother programme. Female sea otters living at the aquarium are introduced to orphaned pups when their behaviour suggests they can provide appropriate maternal care. The surrogate mothers teach the pups skills that are difficult to learn from humans. These include diving, foraging, grooming and resting in the natural way. Staff members monitor the relationship while minimising direct contact and providing enrichment. After reaching important behavioural milestones, the young otters are released into the wild. Over the lifetime of the programme, the aquarium has cared for more than 1,000 stranded sea otters and surrogate-raised 84 pups.Why sea otters matter to coastal ecosystemsSea otters are considered a keystone species because their feeding behaviour can influence the health of an entire coastal ecosystem. By eating certain marine invertebrates, they can help maintain kelp forests and eelgrass meadows. The aquarium’s work in Elkhorn Slough offers an example of this wider impact. Between 2001 and 2016, the team released 37 surrogate-reared sea otters into the estuary. The aquarium reports that those animals and their offspring accounted for more than half of the population growth during that period.The recovering otter population helped reduce numbers of invasive non-native crabs. With fewer crabs consuming sea slugs, the slugs were able to eat algae that might otherwise have overwhelmed eelgrass. As eelgrass recovered, it helped stabilise shorelines, reduce erosion and improve water quality. The sequence shows how rescuing individual animals can eventually support habitats and other species.A conservation legacy that continuesThe aquarium’s work now covers coastal California wildlife, sustainable fisheries, plastic pollution and climate change. Its Seafood Watch programme promotes more responsible fishing and aquaculture, while its public campaigns encourage action on plastic waste and ocean warming. Education remains central to that mission. The aquarium hosts school field trips, trains teachers and provides programmes for teenagers interested in science and ocean leadership. These initiatives connect visitors with marine life while giving them practical ways to understand environmental problems. The $57 million gift that opened the aquarium was therefore more than a construction contribution. It helped create an institution where public fascination could support scientific research and conservation.From a former cannery site, the Monterey Bay Aquarium has become a place where visitors can see ocean life up close, while researchers and conservationists work to protect it outside the building. Its sea otter programme captures that mission clearly. By caring for stranded animals, raising pups with surrogate mothers and returning them to the coast, the aquarium is helping restore not only a vulnerable species but also the ecosystems that depend on it.

articles.title: A uranium mill left radioactive waste beside Utah’s Colorado River for decades; after trains began hauling it away in 2009, crews have now removed 17 million tons to a disposal site 30 miles away
articles.summary: For decades, millions of tons of uranium mill tailings sat beside the Colorado River near Moab, Utah, leaving behind a major environmental cleanup
articles.body: For decades, millions of tons of uranium mill tailings sat beside the Colorado River near Moab, Utah, leaving behind a major environmental cleanup challenge in a landscape known for its red rock scenery and tourism. The waste came from a uranium processing site that operated during the Cold War era, and concerns grew over contamination near the river. According to the U.S. Department of Energy, crews began transporting the tailings by rail in 2009 to an engineered disposal cell about 30 miles away in Crescent Junction. In September 2026, the Moab Uranium Mill Tailings Remedial Action Project marked a major milestone: 17 million tons had been removed from the riverbanks.How the waste reached the riverbankThe material left near Moab was uranium mill tailings, the sand-like waste produced after uranium-bearing ore is processed. Although the tailings do not resemble the bright yellow uranium compounds often shown in popular culture, they can contain radioactive materials and other contaminants that require long-term management. The former Moab uranium mill operated near the Colorado River, an important waterway that supplies communities, supports agriculture and carries water through some of the American Southwest’s most environmentally sensitive landscapes.When the mill closed, the tailings remained at the site. For many years, the waste was stored in a large pile close to the river. Its location created concern because wind, erosion, flooding and groundwater movement could potentially carry contaminants away from the original site. The material was not treated like ordinary construction debris. It required a carefully planned removal process that could protect workers, nearby communities, transportation routes and the river corridor.Rail transport began in 2009The Department of Energy began moving the tailings by rail in 2009. Rather than carrying the waste by truck through surrounding communities and roads, the project used specially managed rail shipments to transport it from the Moab Site to Crescent Junction. The disposal cell is located approximately 30 miles away. It was engineered specifically to contain the material and reduce the possibility that water, wind or erosion could spread contamination. Moving 17 million tons is a logistical operation on a massive scale. Crews have had to excavate the tailings, load the material into rail containers, transport it to the disposal location and place it inside the engineered cell.Each stage involves monitoring and safety controls. The work must also account for changing weather, equipment maintenance, rail scheduling and the need to prevent dust or contaminated material from escaping during handling.Why the location mattersThe proximity of the tailings pile to the Colorado River made the Moab cleanup especially important. The river is not only a major regional water source, but also a defining feature of the surrounding environment. Moab is known for its national parks, desert landscapes and outdoor recreation. The river corridor supports wildlife and provides a route through a region where water is already limited. Protecting the area requires attention to both visible pollution and contamination that may move through soil or groundwater.The Department of Energy’s project is intended to remove the large surface pile and address contamination beneath and next to it. Removing the material reduces the risk associated with leaving a radioactive waste pile in place beside the river. However, the completion of the main removal milestone does not mean every part of the cleanup is finished. The site still requires monitoring, construction and restoration work.What remains to be doneAccording to the Department of Energy, crews will continue developing and implementing a final groundwater compliance action plan. This work will determine how groundwater conditions are monitored and managed over the long term. The project also includes removing contaminated soil beneath and adjacent to the original surface tailings pile. Even after the visible waste has been transported away, material beneath the pile may require excavation or other treatment.Officials must also demonstrate compliance with radiological standards. That process involves testing and documentation to confirm that the site meets the requirements established for cleanup and long-term management. Other remaining tasks include disposing of equipment and infrastructure used during the project, completing the cover over the Crescent Junction disposal cell and stabilising the Moab site. Final stabilisation is expected to involve regrading the surface and revegetating the area so that it is less vulnerable to erosion.Building a long-term disposal cellThe Crescent Junction site is designed to contain the tailings for the long term. Its cover will play an important role in managing moisture and protecting the disposal cell’s integrity. Water is a major concern in the management of radioactive waste. If rain or melting snow enters a waste pile, it can move contaminants through the soil and potentially into groundwater. A properly designed cover helps limit infiltration and reduces exposure to weather and erosion.The cover also needs to remain effective over many years. That means engineers must consider settlement, drainage, vegetation, surface runoff and the effects of extreme weather. Long-term disposal is therefore more than placing the tailings in a hole and covering them. It requires a stable design, monitoring systems and a plan for maintaining the site after active cleanup crews have left.A milestone, not the final chapterThe removal of 17 million tons is a major achievement for the Moab Uranium Mill Tailings Remedial Action Project. It marks the movement of an enormous amount of radioactive waste away from the banks of the Colorado River and into a purpose-built disposal facility. The milestone also shows why environmental cleanup projects can take decades. The mill closed long ago, but the waste remained a complex responsibility for government agencies, engineers, workers and surrounding communities.For people living near the Colorado River, the project offers the possibility of a safer and more stable landscape. For officials responsible for the cleanup, the next phase will be focused on groundwater, remaining contaminated soil, the disposal cell cover and final restoration.The pile that once dominated the riverbank is gradually disappearing from the Moab landscape. Yet the project’s success will ultimately be measured not only by the amount of waste removed, but by whether the disposal site remains secure and the former mill property can be stabilised for generations to come.

articles.title: Burmese python mothers can generate heat while guarding their eggs; scientists documented the behaviour in a wild Florida nest
articles.summary: A Burmese python guarding a clutch of eggs may appear to be doing little more than lying tightly coiled around them.
articles.body: A Burmese python guarding a clutch of eggs may appear to be doing little more than lying tightly coiled around them. In fact, the female can play an active role in controlling the temperature inside the nest. When conditions become too cool, muscles along her body begin contracting rapidly, producing heat that raises her own temperature and helps warm the eggs. The behaviour has been known from controlled observations, but a later field study captured it in a wild Burmese python nest in Florida. Temperature loggers placed around the nest recorded changes in the conditions surrounding the female, while video provided a direct record of her shivering movements.Burmese python mothers stay coiled around their eggs for two monthsBurmese python females remain with their eggs throughout incubation, a period that lasts roughly two months. During this time, the female does not feed. Her body instead remains wrapped around the clutch, creating a close physical barrier between the eggs and the surrounding environment.That arrangement does more than keep the eggs together. The female's own body can influence the temperature they experience. Earlier measurements of a brooding Burmese python showed that her body temperature and metabolic rate changed when the surrounding temperature dropped below about 33°C, according to the study published in Science titled, ‘Thermoregulation in a Brooding Female Indian Python, Python molurus bivittatus’.At those lower temperatures, the muscles of the snake began making spasmodic contractions. The activity increased her metabolic rate and produced additional body heat. In effect, the python was using muscular activity to warm herself while remaining over the eggs.How Burmese pythons heat their eggsThe mechanism is unusual because Burmese pythons, like other reptiles, generally rely heavily on external sources of heat to regulate their body temperature. A brooding female has a different option available while she is confined to the nest.The contractions observed during incubation generated enough heat to raise the female's body temperature. Because she was tightly positioned around the clutch, that warmth could also affect the eggs immediately beneath and around her.Earlier physiological work concluded that the process allowed a brooding Burmese python to regulate its temperature through a mechanism comparable in some respects to physiological heat production in endothermic animals. The snake was not simply choosing a warmer place for its eggs.Scientists capture the python heating its nest in the wildThe field observation in Florida added an important piece of evidence because the behaviour was documented outside controlled laboratory conditions. The study involved a brooding Python molurus bivittatus, the scientific name used for the Burmese python in the report, at a site just north of Everglades National Park.According to the study published in BioOne Digital Library, titled ‘Thermoregulation by a Brooding Burmese Python (Python Molurus Bivittatus) in Florida’ reveals that the researchers placed temperature data loggers both within the nest and around the brooding female. Video equipment was also used to record what the snake was doing. This combination allowed them to compare the temperature inside the nesting area with conditions immediately outside it while watching the female's behaviour.The recordings showed the python performing the muscular contractions associated with shivering thermogenesis. The temperature measurements also indicated that the nest did not simply mirror the surrounding air. Conditions inside it could be warmer or cooler than the ambient temperature.How the brooding female helps regulate nest temperatureThe female's body is only part of the system. Her position over the eggs can provide insulation, reducing the direct influence of changes in the surrounding environment. A sudden drop in the conditions around a nest can alter the thermal environment experienced by the clutch. By remaining tightly coiled and producing heat when necessary, the female can influence that environment without leaving the eggs.The Florida observation therefore brought together two behaviours: heat production through muscular contractions and insulation provided by the brooding female. Both were observed at the same wild nest.A different role for a brooding pythonThe behaviour also changes how the female's long period of nest attendance can be understood. Her presence is not limited to physical protection of the eggs. She can actively alter the thermal conditions around them. The female remains with the clutch for the incubation period without feeding, while the muscular activity involved in generating heat requires additional energy. The measurements taken from brooding females showed that shivering was accompanied by an increase in metabolic rate.For the eggs, however, the arrangement provides a way of maintaining a more controlled environment than the surrounding conditions might otherwise allow.The female python also defends her nest from predatorsTemperature control is not the only behaviour associated with brooding. A separate observation in the Everglades documented a female responding when a bobcat approached an unguarded python nest.The bobcat had been photographed raiding the nest while the female was away. When the python returned, it displayed active defensive behaviour towards the predator. The encounter was significant because it provided a documented record of a Burmese python defending its eggs against a mammalian predator in Florida.Taken together, the observations show that a brooding female can have several roles during the same period of her reproductive cycle. She remains with the eggs, alters their thermal surroundings through her own body and can respond to threats near the nest.

articles.title: In 2021, scientists released fluorescent dye 1,870 metres deep in the North Atlantic; tracking it revealed canyon water rising about 100 metres a day, around 10,000 times the global average
articles.summary: A fluorescent green dye released nearly 1,870 metres below the surface of the North Atlantic has helped scientists directly observe a long-suspected
articles.body: A fluorescent green dye released nearly 1,870 metres below the surface of the North Atlantic has helped scientists directly observe a long-suspected movement of deep ocean water, and the water was rising far faster at the study site than the global average previously estimated.In an experiment conducted in 2021, researchers released about 55 gallons of non-toxic fluorescein dye close to the seafloor inside a submarine canyon in the Rockall Trough, roughly 370 kilometres northwest of Ireland. By tracking the dye as it moved through the deep water, the team found evidence of vigorous upward mixing along the canyon slope.The measured upwelling was of the order of 100 metres per day, around 10,000 times the global average rate required to sustain the ocean's large-scale overturning circulation, according to the study published in Nature in June 2024. The finding addresses a long-standing question in oceanography: how does cold, dense water that sinks into the deep ocean eventually return towards the surface?A mystery hidden deep beneath the oceanThe world's oceans are constantly moving heat, carbon and nutrients through a vast circulation system. Cold, dense seawater forms at high latitudes, particularly around Antarctica, sinks into the deep ocean and eventually has to rise again as part of the global overturning circulation. This return journey, known as upwelling, is essential to the ocean's circulation and its role in regulating Earth's climate.But directly observing deep-water upwelling has been difficult. In 1966, oceanographer Walter Munk estimated that the global average rate of deep-water upwelling was about 1 centimetre per day. Spread across the enormous volume of the world's oceans, such movement would involve huge amounts of water but would be extremely difficult to measure directly.Scientists had subsequently gathered evidence suggesting that turbulence near the seafloor could help drive the process. However, observations had not provided a direct measurement of vigorous upward movement of deep water along underwater slopes. This is what changed with the dye experiment.55 gallons of dye released almost 2 km deepThe researchers selected a submarine canyon within the Rockall Trough, an area of deep ocean with steep underwater terrain. The canyon itself is about 32 kilometres long and has walls rising hundreds of metres above its deepest channel. The team lowered a 55-gallon drum containing fluorescein to about 10 metres above the canyon floor before remotely releasing the dye.At the release point, the water was 1,870 metres deep and had a temperature of about 3.53°C, according to the Nature paper. Scientists then followed the dye for roughly three days using instruments designed to detect extremely small concentrations of the fluorescent substance.Among them were fluorometers capable of detecting the dye at concentrations of less than one part per billion. Other instruments measured temperature, water movement and turbulent mixing, allowing researchers to track not only where the dye travelled but also the physical conditions around it.Water rose far faster than the global averageThe measurements showed that the dye was being transported upward across density layers near the canyon floor. The researchers calculated several estimates of the upwelling rate. They ranged from about 51 to 325 metres per day, but all indicated significant upwelling on the order of 100 metres per day. The study's analysis gave an average estimate of about 125 metres per day, with an uncertainty of 31 metres per day, while another method based on the dye's change in height produced a lower estimate of 64 metres per day.The important point is that the experiment did not show that all deep ocean water rises at 100 metres per day.Instead, it captured an unusually rapid process in a specific setting, a sloping submarine canyon where turbulence and internal tides interact with the seafloor.The roughly 10,000-fold comparison comes from contrasting the observed rate at the canyon with the global-average rate of about 1 centimetre per day used in earlier estimates of the circulation's requirements.Why underwater canyons matterThe study suggests that the shape of the ocean floor may play a much larger role in deep-water circulation than previously understood. As tides move over underwater topography, they can generate internal waves within the ocean. In the Rockall Trough canyon, these internal tides interact with the steep seafloor and can break, producing intense turbulence.The researchers observed strong along-canyon flows and vertical movements of water associated with these processes. The canyon's slopes appear to provide conditions where turbulent mixing can drive deep water upward across density layers.This helps address an apparent problem in earlier explanations of ocean circulation. Turbulence is often stronger close to the seafloor, but simply assuming that mixing increases uniformly towards the bottom does not adequately explain how the deep ocean gets rid of the cold, dense water that continually forms at high latitudes.The new observations support the idea that steep underwater features such as canyons can act as hotspots where mixing produces rapid upwelling.What the discovery means for climate researchThe researchers say the findings could eventually improve climate models. The ocean absorbs and redistributes enormous quantities of heat and carbon, making its circulation an important part of Earth's climate system. If important portions of that circulation occur through relatively concentrated hotspots around seafloor features, models need to accurately represent those processes.However, one experiment cannot establish how common the phenomenon is throughout the world's oceans. The Rockall Trough canyon was deliberately chosen because it was considered relatively typical rather than an extreme geological feature. The researchers said this raises the possibility that similar processes could occur in other submarine canyons, but further observations are needed to determine how widespread they are.The team has also been conducting another dye-release experiment near the Scripps Institution of Oceanography campus in the La Jolla submarine canyon, aiming to investigate whether comparable upwelling occurs in a different setting.For now, the 2021 experiment provides something oceanographers had lacked for decades: direct observations of vigorous deep-ocean upwelling along a sloping submarine canyon.
